_comment: Plain-language glossary and sentence templates of the farmer advisor. Every term has reviewed=false until an agronomist or extension agent has checked the wording (see farmer-advisor-plan.md, Review TODO). Wording is drafted from the repo's own definitions (docstrings, explorer/schema.py comments), no new domain facts.

water.short: How much irrigation water the rotation needs, per day.
water.long: The irrigation water the crops need on top of rain, averaged over every day of one pass through the rotation and over past weather years (1991-2025). The model is a daily soil water balance after FAO-56. The score runs from 0 (needs the least water of all tested rotations) to 1 (needs the most).
water.unit: score 0-1 (0 = best); raw value in the details is inches of irrigation per day
water.why_it_matters: Irrigation costs money and, in dry regions, water is limited.
water.source: FAO-56 via the Field Shift scorer

risk.short: How often heat, cold or frost hurt the crops of this rotation.
risk.long: A daily risk value for each crop on the days it stands in the field: it grows when the day is hotter or colder than the crop likes, and jumps on days that are cold enough to kill the crop. Days without a crop (fallow) carry no risk. The score runs from 0 (lowest risk of all tested rotations) to 1 (highest).
risk.why_it_matters: Heat and frost are a main reason for a bad harvest, and they cannot be fixed afterwards.
risk.source: FAO Ecocrop temperature limits, NASA POWER weather, via the Field Shift scorer

soil_health.short: How much of the time the soil is left bare.
soil_health.long: The share of days in the rotation's window on which the field has neither a main crop nor a cover crop. Bare soil is open to wind and water erosion. The score runs from 0 (least bare time of all tested rotations) to 1 (most).
soil_health.unit: score 0-1 (0 = best); raw value is the share of bare days
soil_health.why_it_matters: Covered soil loses less topsoil. A cover crop between two main crops reduces the bare time.
soil_health.source: Field Shift scorer (bare days as erosion indicator)

nitrogen.short: How much nitrogen fertilizer the rotation needs, per day.
nitrogen.long: The nitrogen fertilizer the crops need, summed over the seasons of one pass and divided by the days of the window. It follows the K-State recommendation (MF2586): it depends on the expected yield, the soil's organic matter, and the crop before. Soybean is assumed to need no fertilizer because it fixes its own nitrogen. After a cover crop of triticale the next crop needs more nitrogen. The score runs from 0 (needs the least) to 1 (needs the most). Today only this score exists; nitrogen amounts per season and month are not computed yet.
nitrogen.why_it_matters: Fertilizer is a large cost and too much of it can leave the field with the water.
nitrogen.source: K-State MF2586 via the Field Shift scorer

score.short: 0 is the best and 1 the worst of all tested rotations, per criterion.
score.long: Each criterion (water, risk, soil cover, nitrogen) is rescaled so that the best of the tested rotations gets 0 and the worst gets 1. A score is therefore a comparison with the other tested rotations, not an absolute grade. The total score is the weighted mean of the four criteria.
score.why_it_matters: A low score means 'better than the others tested', it does not promise a yield or a profit.

weights.short: How much each criterion counts in the ranking.
weights.long: The total score is the weighted mean of the four criterion scores. Only the ratio of the weights matters: 2, 1, 1, 1 means water counts twice as much as each other criterion. A weight of 0 switches a criterion off.
weights.why_it_matters: Your priorities decide the ranking. A farmer with little water will weight water higher.

rank.short: The place in the ranking; the top 3 are shown as picks.
rank.long: All tested rotations are ordered by total score. 'Pick 1-3' marks the three best that have a full detailed view (seasons, yields, months). Other rotations only have their scores.
rank.why_it_matters: The rank depends on the weights you choose.

rotation.short: The order of crops over the seasons, for example corn, soybean, sorghum.
rotation.long: A rotation here is three main crops in a row from corn, sorghum, soybean, winter wheat and sunflower, optionally with a triticale cover crop in the gaps where it fits. The id looks like 'corn-soybean-sorghum+triticale'. The scorer tests all combinations and plays each one through every start year with past weather.
rotation.why_it_matters: Which crop follows which affects water, nitrogen, yield and soil cover.

window.short: The time from the first sowing to the last harvest of one pass.
window.long: All scores are measured over this window and divided by its days, so rotations of different length can be compared. The first and last month of the window can be partial.
window.why_it_matters: It explains why the first and last month show lower values than the months in between.

et0.short: How much water the weather alone would evaporate from a standard grass field.
et0.long: ET0 is the water a well-watered standard grass surface loses to the air through evaporation and plant leaves, calculated from the weather. It is the starting point of the water model: the crop's own water use (ETc) is ET0 times a crop factor. In the data ET0 is shown for April to September.
et0.why_it_matters: ET0 minus rain tells how much water is missing in a season.

etc.short: How much water the crop actually uses.
etc.long: ETc is ET0 multiplied by a crop factor (Kc) that changes with the crop's growth stage. In explorer.json it is the field 'et_in': crop water use per month; in a bare month it is only evaporation from bare soil.
etc.why_it_matters: Whatever rain does not cover of the crop's water use has to come from irrigation or from the soil's stored water.

ks.short: How much a lack of water holds the crop back.
ks.long: In the water model the crop uses less than ETc when the soil runs dry. The ratio between actual and wanted water use is the basis of the yield loss in dry years. You will mostly meet its effect in the yield spread, not the factor itself.
ks.why_it_matters: Dry years are the reason why the yield range (p10 to p90) is wide for rain-fed seasons.
ks.source: FAO-56, yield response idea of FAO-33, via explorer/yields.py

spread.short: The average and the range of a value over past weather years.
spread.long: 'v' is the mean over all weather years (1991-2025). 'p10' is the value that only the lowest 10% of the years fell below, 'p90' the value that only the highest 10% of the years exceeded. So 8 out of 10 years fall between p10 and p90. The mean is used (not the median) so that months add up exactly to the season.
spread.why_it_matters: A wide range means that the value differs a lot from year to year.

irr_in.long: Per season it is a mean with p10/p90 range from the scorer's water balance with the season's irrigation level applied; per month it is the mean over the weather years. It is zero if the irrigation level is 'none'.
irr_in.why_it_matters: It is the water you would have to pump, and a main driver of the water score.

irrigation.short: Full, reduced or none: how much of the water need you irrigate.
irrigation.long: 'full' means all water the crop needs beyond rain is supplied. 'reduced' means half of that. 'none' means rain-fed. The level in the data is an assumption (currently full), not your own choice.
irrigation.why_it_matters: Yield and water use change strongly with the level. Reduced is an assumption of 50% of full.

elevation_ft.short: How high the field lies above sea level.
elevation_ft.long: Taken from the USGS 3DEP elevation model (10 m resolution).
elevation_ft.why_it_matters: Height influences temperature and so the frost and heat risk.

slope_pct.long: Slope in percent: 1 means a drop of 1 foot over 100 feet. Taken from the USGS 3DEP elevation model.
slope_pct.why_it_matters: Steeper fields lose more soil to water erosion.

crop_history.short: Which crops grew on the field in past years.
crop_history.long: Read from the USDA satellite crop maps (Cropland Data Layer), one crop per year. The map can misjudge a crop, and some years show classes such as fallow or idle land.
crop_history.why_it_matters: It sets what the crop before the first season was and so the 'current rotation'.

previous_crop.short: The crop that grew on the field before the first season.
previous_crop.long: Taken from the satellite crop maps, not from your own records. It affects the nitrogen need and the yield of the first season.
previous_crop.why_it_matters: A legume such as soybean before a crop saves fertilizer; the same crop twice can cost yield.

rotation_start_year.short: The year of the first sowing in the display.
rotation_start_year.long: The dates in the data are moved to this year so the three seasons follow each other. It is an assumption for display, the scores use all weather years 1991-2025.
rotation_start_year.why_it_matters: It does not change the ranking, only the dates shown.

heat_days_ge_35.term: Hot days (35 degrees C and above)
heat_days_ge_35.short: Days per year with a highest temperature of 35 degrees C or more.
heat_days_ge_35.long: A count per year from NASA POWER weather. It describes the climate of the field and is not tied to a crop.
heat_days_ge_35.why_it_matters: Many hot days raise the heat stress risk of the crops and the irrigation need.

deficit_apr_sep_in.short: ET0 minus rain over the growing season; positive means water is missing.
deficit_apr_sep_in.long: The difference between what the weather would evaporate (ET0) and the rain, summed from April to September, per year.
deficit_apr_sep_in.why_it_matters: Shows how much irrigation a normal grass-like crop would need in each year.

rain_in.short: The rain that falls in a month, as a mean over past years.
rain_in.long: Rain is taken from NASA POWER daily weather (about 50 km grid) and averaged over the weather years.
rain_in.why_it_matters: Rain reduces the irrigation need. Grid data can differ from your own rain gauge.

et_in.short: What the crop uses in a month; on bare months only evaporation.
et_in.long: See ETc. The monthly value is the mean over all weather years.
et_in.why_it_matters: It shows in which months the water demand peaks.
et_in.source: FAO-56 via the Field Shift scorer

m.short: The calendar month of the rotation window, as YYYY-MM.
m.long: One row per month from the first sowing to the last harvest. Values are means over the weather years.
m.why_it_matters: Lets you see when in the year the water and risk values fall.

kind.short: Crop, cover or bare: what covers the field in that month.
kind.long: 'crop' means a main crop stands most days of the month, 'cover' a cover crop, 'bare' neither.
kind.why_it_matters: Bare months are the ones with erosion risk.
kind.source: Field Shift scorer (rule: what stands on most days)

crop.short: The crop that stands in the field.
crop.long: One of corn, sorghum, soybean, winter wheat, sunflower, or the cover crop triticale. In a month, it is the crop that stands on most days.

year.short: The year in which the season is harvested.
year.long: Winter crops such as winter wheat are planted in the autumn before their harvest year.
year.why_it_matters: Avoids confusion when the sowing and the harvest are in different years.

plant_date.short: When the crop is sown, from the typical calendar.
plant_date.long: Dates come from the USDA NASS crop calendar for Kansas and are a rule, not your own plan.
plant_date.why_it_matters: Sowing time decides which weather the crop meets.

harvest_date.short: When the crop is harvested, from the typical calendar.
harvest_date.long: Dates come from the USDA NASS crop calendar for Kansas and are a rule, not your own plan.

cover.short: Whether a cover crop (triticale) grows in the gap after this season.

cover_crop.short: A crop grown between two main crops to keep the soil covered.
cover_crop.long: The scorer tests every rotation with and without a triticale cover crop, where a gap is long enough. The cover crop uses soil water, so it can raise the water need, and it is not bare soil, so it improves the soil cover score. After a cereal cover crop the next crop needs more nitrogen, because the residue ties up nitrogen.
cover_crop.why_it_matters: It trades some water and nitrogen for less erosion.
cover_crop.source: Field Shift scorer; Clark (ed.) 2007, Managing Cover Crops Profitably, SARE, for the nitrogen effect

yield.short: The yield to expect, with a range over past weather years.
yield.long: The yield level comes from USDA NASS statistics for the county (full irrigation or rain-fed). A water deficit of the season reduces it, and literature effects of the crop order (for example corn after corn) raise or lower it. The range p10 to p90 comes from the weather years. This is a model result, not a forecast.
yield.unit: bushels per acre, or pounds per acre (shown in the unit field)
yield.why_it_matters: It is the base of any income estimate, with the range showing the bad-year risk.
yield.source: USDA NASS Quick Stats; FAO-33 idea via explorer/yields.py

yield_pct_rotation.term: Yield compared with the crop's reference
yield_pct_rotation.short: How the season's yield compares with the typical yield of that crop, in percent.
yield_pct_rotation.long: 100% is the typical yield of the crop at the same irrigation level. Below or above 100% comes from water carry-over in the rotation and from literature effects of the crop order.
yield_pct_rotation.why_it_matters: Shows whether this position in the rotation helps or hurts the crop.

effects.short: Yield effects of the crop order found in studies.
effects.long: For example a yield drag for corn after corn. Every effect carries its source and a label of how reliable it is (see provenance labels).
effects.why_it_matters: Studies come from other regions, so treat them as a rough guide for your field.
effects.source: Seifert, Roberts & Lobell 2017; NDSU Sunflower Production Guide

n_lb.short: The nitrogen fertilizer recommended for the season.
n_lb.long: Planned after the K-State recommendation for the crop. It is not computed yet and shows as missing until the nitrogen work package is delivered.
n_lb.why_it_matters: A main cost item; missing values mean only the nitrogen score exists.

n_adj_lb.short: More or less fertilizer because of the crop before.
n_adj_lb.long: After a legume such as soybean the next crop needs less fertilizer, so the value can be negative. Not computed yet, shows as missing.
n_adj_lb.why_it_matters: It is the nitrogen benefit of a good crop order.

fert_lb.short: Nitrogen fertilizer put on the field in the month.
fert_lb.long: Part of a monthly nitrogen balance. Not computed yet.

uptake_lb.short: Nitrogen taken up by the crop in the month.
uptake_lb.long: Part of a monthly nitrogen balance. Not computed yet.

fix_lb.short: Nitrogen that a legume such as soybean takes from the air.
fix_lb.long: Part of a monthly nitrogen balance. Not computed yet.
fix_lb.why_it_matters: Free nitrogen for the legume and, partly, for the next crop.

credit_lb.short: Nitrogen made available from the soil or the previous crop.
credit_lb.long: Part of a monthly nitrogen balance. Not computed yet.

pool_lb.short: Nitrogen available in the soil at the end of the month.
pool_lb.long: Part of a monthly nitrogen balance. Not computed yet.

loss_lb.short: Nitrogen that leaves the field, for example with drainage water.
loss_lb.long: Part of a monthly nitrogen balance. Not computed yet.
loss_lb.why_it_matters: Lost nitrogen is paid for but does not feed the crop.

short_lb.short: Nitrogen the crop needed but did not get.
short_lb.long: Part of a monthly nitrogen balance. Not computed yet.

n_loss_lb.short: Nitrogen lost from the field over the whole rotation.
n_loss_lb.long: Sum of the monthly losses. Not computed yet, shows as missing.

bare_months.short: Months per year in which the field has neither crop nor cover crop.
bare_months.long: A mean over the window. It is the same idea as the soil cover score, but in months.
bare_months.why_it_matters: Fewer bare months mean less erosion risk.

same_crop_repeats.term: Same crop twice in a row
same_crop_repeats.short: How many seasons follow the same crop as the one before.
same_crop_repeats.long: The first season is compared with the crop before the rotation (your field's previous crop).
same_crop_repeats.why_it_matters: Same-crop repeats can build up disease and pests and often cost some yield.

heat_years_pct.short: In how many of the past years the month had at least one too-hot day.
heat_years_pct.long: A heat day is a day whose highest temperature is above the optimum of the crop in the field. The value is the share of weather years with at least one such day in that month.
heat_years_pct.why_it_matters: Heat in sensitive months can cut the yield.
heat_years_pct.source: FAO Ecocrop limits, NASA POWER weather

cold_stress_years_pct.short: In how many of the past years the month had at least one cold day for the crop.
cold_stress_years_pct.long: A cold-stress day is a day on which the temperature stayed below the crop's optimum for at least half of the day. It is less severe than a killing frost. The half-day rule is our own assumption, not a standard threshold.
cold_stress_years_pct.why_it_matters: Cool spells slow growth, for example after early sowing.
cold_stress_years_pct.source: FAO Ecocrop limits, NASA POWER weather; half-day rule is an assumption

kill_years_pct.short: In how many of the past years the month had a day cold enough to kill the crop.
kill_years_pct.long: A kill day is a day below the crop's killing temperature, which means real frost damage. The value is the share of weather years with at least one such day in that month.
kill_years_pct.why_it_matters: This is the most severe temperature risk, because the crop may have to be re-sown or is lost.
kill_years_pct.source: FAO Ecocrop limits, NASA POWER weather

nitrogen_pending.short: Only the nitrogen score exists, the amounts in pounds are not computed yet.
nitrogen_pending.long: The nitrogen amounts per season and month, and the nitrogen loss, are still missing in the data. Treat the nitrogen score as the only available nitrogen information.
nitrogen_pending.why_it_matters: Do not read a missing value as zero.

placeholder.short: Values that are still demo values and not the real results.
placeholder.long: If a rotation is marked as placeholder, its numbers are mock-up values to test the display. Do not use them for decisions.
placeholder.why_it_matters: A placeholder can look real but is not.

measured.short: Taken from real observations, such as weather or soil surveys.
measured.long: Example: rain from NASA POWER, soil from USDA SSURGO, elevation from USGS. Measured data can still be a coarse grid value for your area.
measured.why_it_matters: The most reliable kind of value here.

modeled.short: Calculated by a model from measured data.
modeled.long: Example: irrigation need from the FAO-56 water balance, or yield from the yield model. Model results follow from past weather and assumptions, they are not forecasts.
modeled.why_it_matters: Good for comparing rotations, less exact for a single year.

rule.short: Set by a fixed rule, for example the typical sowing calendar.
rule.long: Example: sowing and harvest dates from the USDA NASS crop calendar, or 'which crop stands on most days of a month'.
rule.why_it_matters: A rule is a simplification; your own dates may differ.

assumption.short: An assumption we made, not a measurement and not your input.
assumption.long: Example: the irrigation level of each season, the year the first sowing takes place, and the half-day rule for cold stress. The result changes if the assumption does not fit your field.
assumption.why_it_matters: These are the values you should check first.

water.mid: needs a medium amount of irrigation water
water.bad: needs a lot of irrigation water

risk.good: has a low risk of heat, cold and frost damage
risk.mid: has a medium risk of heat, cold and frost damage
risk.bad: has a high risk of heat, cold and frost damage

soil_health.good: keeps the soil covered most of the time
soil_health.mid: leaves the soil bare for part of the time
soil_health.bad: leaves the soil bare for long stretches (erosion risk)

nitrogen.mid: needs a medium amount of nitrogen fertilizer
nitrogen.bad: needs a lot of nitrogen fertilizer

trade_off_phrases.risk: has a lower risk of heat, cold and frost damage
trade_off_phrases.soil_health: keeps the soil covered more of the time

templates.trade_off_none: The two rotations are close on all four criteria.
templates.explain_summary: {name} is place {rank} of {n} tested rotations with your weights. Its strongest point: it {best}. Its weakest point: it {worst}.
templates.explain_summary_single: {name} is place {rank} of {n} tested rotations with your weights. Only one criterion counts: it {best}.
templates.explain_relative: Scores compare the {n} tested rotations with each other (0 = best, 1 = worst). They are not an absolute grade and not a promise of yield or profit.

caveats.relative_scores: Scores compare the {n} tested rotations with each other (0 = best, 1 = worst). They are not an absolute grade and not a promise of yield or profit.
caveats.scores_only: This rotation only has scores. There are no seasons, yields, nitrogen amounts or monthly values for it.
caveats.placeholder: The values of this rotation are placeholder (demo) values, not the real results. Do not use them for decisions.
caveats.placeholder_unknown: It is not known whether the scores of this rotation are final, because it has no detailed view.
caveats.nitrogen_pending: Nitrogen amounts in pounds are not computed yet, only the nitrogen score exists. A missing amount does not mean zero.
caveats.modeled: Yields, irrigation and stress values are model results based on past weather ({first_year}-{last_year}). They are not forecasts.
caveats.literature_effect: The yield effect of the crop order comes from a study in another region ({title}). Treat it as a rough guide.
caveats.grid_weather: Weather comes from a coarse grid (about 50 km), not from a station at your field.

assumptions.field.previous_crop: The crop before the first season comes from satellite crop maps (USDA CDL), not from your own records.
assumptions.field.rotation_start_year: The year of the first sowing is assumed, not chosen by you.
assumptions.sequence.irrigation: The irrigation level of each season ({levels}) is an assumption, not your own choice.
assumptions.monthly.cold_stress_years_pct: Cold stress is our own rule (below the crop's best temperature for at least half a day), not a standard threshold.
